heroData.title: EOR & PEO in Djibouti
heroData.subtitle: Hire compliant teams in Djibouti without a local entity
heroData.description: Establish a presence in Djibouti using Employer of Record (EOR) services to bypass entity setup requirements while remaining compliant with the Labor Code. Our EOR partners handle all legal liabilities, payroll coordination, and HR administration.
heroData.bestFor: Logistics companies, international NGOs, and defense contractors expanding into the Horn of Africa

sections.title: EOR Onboarding Process
sections.subtitle: Steps to deploy talent in Djibouti

steps.title: Requirement Analysis & Scope Definition
steps.description: Define the scope of work, job description, and salary in Djiboutian Francs (DJF). Confirm if the role requires a local national or an expatriate hire, as this affects the timeline and cost.

steps.title: Candidate Selection & Screening
steps.description: Select the candidate. The EOR will then conduct necessary background checks and collect employee identification documents (National ID for locals, Passport for expats).

steps.title: KYC & Compliance Documentation
steps.description: Both the client and the employee must submit KYC documents. The EOR prepares the tripartite agreement ensuring all local labor laws (Code du Travail) are met.

steps.title: Contract Issuance
steps.description: Issue a localized employment contract (Contrat de Travail) in French or Arabic. English versions are provided for clarity but the French/Arabic version prevails in court.

steps.title: Social Security Registration (OPS/CNSS)
steps.description: The EOR registers the employee with the Organisme de Protection Sociale (OPS) / Caisse Nationale de Sécurité Sociale (CNSS) for mandatory health and pension coverage.

steps.title: Work Permit Processing (Expats Only)
steps.description: For foreign staff, the EOR sponsors the Entry Visa and subsequent Carte de Séjour (Residence Card) and Work Permit (Carte de Travail).

steps.title: Onboarding & Payroll Setup
steps.description: Employee is inducted into the local payroll system. First month's salary and benefits are calculated/prorated.

rows.label: Social Security (CNSS) - Employer
values: Calculated on gross salary, capped at ceiling

rows.label: Management Fee
values: Monthly per employee depending on volume

rows.label: VAT
values: Applied to management fee and total invoice

items.title: Fixed-Term Contracts (CDD)
items.text: Fixed-term contracts (Contrat à Durée Déterminée) in Djibouti cannot generally exceed 12 months and can only be renewed once. Continued employment thereafter defaults to a permanent contract (CDI).

items.title: Currency Stability
items.text: The Djiboutian Franc (DJF) is pegged to the US Dollar (approx 177.72 DJF = 1 USD). This peg provides significant payroll stability for foreign employers budgeting in USD.

items.title: Language for Contracts
items.text: Employment contracts must be written in French or Arabic. While English translations are common for HQ understanding, they are rarely legally binding in local labor courts.

items.title: Probation Period
items.text: Probation periods are typically 15 days for hourly workers and up to 3 months for executives, renewable once. This must be explicitly stated in the contract.

items.title: Notice Periods
items.text: Notice periods usually range from 1 to 3 months depending on seniority and contract type. Failure to give notice requires payment in lieu.

items.title: Severance Calculation
items.text: Statutory severance is often calculated as a percentage of salary per year of service (e.g., 20-30%), but collective agreements may dictate higher amounts.

items.title: Dismissal Grounds
items.text: Dismissal must be justified (e.g., gross misconduct, economic redundancy). Arbitrary dismissal will likely result in heavy penalties in labor court.

faqs.question: Can I use an EOR for permanent employees?
faqs.answer: Yes, but be aware that permanent establishment risks increase after 12-24 months of operations without a local entity. It is often used as a market entry vehicle.

faqs.question: Is severance pay mandatory?
faqs.answer: Yes, for unjustified dismissal or redundancy. Severance is typically calculated based on length of service (often 20-30% of monthly salary per year of service, but check specific Collective Agreements).

faqs.question: How fast can I hire a local employee?
faqs.answer: Locals can be onboarded in 3-5 days once the contract is signed. The limiting factor is usually the background check and contract negotiation.

faqs.question: How long does it take to hire an expatriate?
faqs.answer: Expatriates require visa processing which can take 2-4 weeks for the entry visa and another 3-6 weeks for the final residence card.

faqs.question: What about the 13th month salary?
faqs.answer: It is not strictly statutory by national law but is mandated by many Collective Bargaining Agreements (CBAs) and is customary in professional sectors.

items.title: Work Week Structure
items.text: The standard work week is Sunday to Thursday (40-48 hours) for the public sector. Many private companies operate Saturday to Thursday or Monday to Friday depending on their interactions with Western markets.

items.title: Prayer Times
items.text: Respect for prayer times is crucial in the workplace. Most employees will take short breaks during the day, especially on Fridays which is the holy day.

items.title: Heat Stress
items.text: During the summer months (June-August), work hours may shift to start earlier (e.g., 7 AM) to avoid the peak heat of the afternoon.

steps.title: Data Collection & Validation
steps.description: Gather attendance data, overtime hours, bonuses, and commission details. Validate changes against HR records by the 20th of the month.

steps.title: Gross-to-Net Calculation
steps.description: Calculate Gross Salary, then deduct ITS (Impôt sur les Traitements et Salaires) based on the progressive tax scale (2% to 30%+) and employee social security.

steps.title: CNSS Declarations
steps.description: Apply 4.5% employee share and ~15.7% employer share for social security contributions. Prepare the declaration files.

steps.title: Net Disbursement
steps.description: Pay employees in DJF via local bank transfer (e.g., BCIMR, Exim Bank, CAC Bank) by month-end (30th/31st).

steps.title: Statutory Filing & Payment
steps.description: Submit monthly declarations and pay withheld taxes to the Tax Department and CNSS contributions by the 15th of the following month.

steps.title: Payslip Distribution
steps.description: Distribute official payslips (Bulletin de Paie) to employees, either physically or digitally.

rows.label: Training Levy
values: Some sectors may apply specific levies

items.title: 13th Month Salary
items.text: A 13th-month bonus is widely expected in professional sectors and normally paid in December or before Eid festivals, though it is not strictly statutory in the Labor Code unless in the CBA.

items.title: Late Filing Penalties
items.text: Fines for late CNSS or Tax filings are steep and strictly enforced, often starting at 5-10% of the due amount plus daily interest.

items.title: Cash vs Bank Payments
items.text: While cash payments are legal for small amounts, bank transfers are mandatory for documented compliance and audits for amounts over certain thresholds to prevent money laundering.

items.title: Payslip Language
items.text: Payslips must be intelligible to the employee, typically in French. They must itemize all deductions clearly.

faqs.question: What is the minimum wage?
faqs.answer: The minimum wage (SMIG) is established by sector (Interprofessional Guaranteed Minimum Wage). For general laborers, it has historically been around 35,000 DJF/month, but collective agreements may set higher floors.

faqs.question: Are transport allowances taxable?
faqs.answer: Transport allowances are generally exempt from ITS up to a reasonable limit defined by tax authorities (often capped).

faqs.question: What is the fiscal year for payroll?
faqs.answer: The fiscal year in Djibouti runs from January 1 to December 31.

faqs.question: How are overtime rates calculated?
faqs.answer: Overtime is typically paid at 125% for the first 8 hours and 150% thereafter, or higher for night/weekend work (check CBA).

faqs.question: Is there a payroll tax on expat allowances?
faqs.answer: Yes, most allowances (housing, school fees) are considered Benefits in Kind and are taxable unless specifically exempted.

items.title: Record Retention
items.text: Payroll records must be kept for at least 5-10 years for tax audits.

items.title: Bank Transfers
items.text: Allow 2-3 business days for local bank transfers to clear if between different banks.

items.title: Confidentiality
items.text: Payroll data is highly sensitive. Ensure access is restricted to authorized personnel only to avoid internal workplace tension.

steps.title: Determine Gross Pay
steps.description: Start with base salary plus taxable allowances.

steps.title: Deduct Social Security
steps.description: Subtract 4.5% employee CNSS contribution.

steps.title: Calculate Taxable Base
steps.description: Gross - CNSS = Taxable Base.

steps.title: Apply Tax Brackets
steps.description: Apply the progressive ITS rates to the Taxable Base.

steps.title: Deduct Tax
steps.description: Subtract the calculated ITS amount.

steps.title: Net Pay
steps.description: Result is the Net Payable to employee.

faqs.question: Is the 13th month taxed?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is generally treated as supplemental income and taxed at the marginal rate.

faqs.question: Are housing allowances taxed?
faqs.answer: Yes, usually added to income base.

faqs.question: Is 13th month mandatory?
faqs.answer: No, but it is a common customary bonus.

faqs.question: Are transport allowances taxable?
faqs.answer: Generally exempt up to a certain limit defined by tax authorities.

items.title: Simulator
items.text: Use the official OTR/CNSS simulators for precise figures.

items.title: Progressive Tax
items.text: Remember ITS is progressive. The top rate of 30%+ applies only to the portion of income above 600,000 DJF.

items.title: Social Security Cap
items.text: CNSS contributions are capped at a monthly salary ceiling (approx 400,000 DJF), beyond which no further % is charged.

items.title: Rounding
items.text: Taxes are usually rounded to the nearest integer.

items.title: Unpaid Leave
items.text: Unpaid leave days reduce the gross salary base for the month, proportionally reducing tax and CNSS.

items.title: Overtime
items.text: Overtime is calculated on the base hourly rate, usually at +25% or +50% rates, and is taxable income.

items.title: Severance Pay
items.text: Severance pay (Indemnité de Licenciement) is generally tax-free up to a certain statutory limit, but check latest Finance Laws.

heroData.title: Incorporation in Djibouti
heroData.subtitle: Set up your SARL or SA in Djibouti
heroData.description: Navigate the ODPIC (Djibouti Office of Industrial and Commercial Property) and One-Stop Shop process to register your business in Djibouti's strategic logistics hub.
heroData.bestFor: Transport, Logistics, Trade companies, and Foreign Investors

steps.title: Name Reservation
steps.description: Obtain a 'Certificat Négatif' from such ODPIC to confirm which your intended company name is unique and available.

steps.title: Draft Statutes & Notarization
steps.description: Prepare the Articles of Association (Statuts) defining the capital, shareholders, and manager. These must be notarized.

steps.title: Capital Deposit
steps.description: Open a 'compte de constitution' at a local bank and deposit the minimum share capital (approx 1M DJF for SARL). Obtain the bank certificate.

steps.title: Registration at Guichet Unique
steps.description: Submit all documents to the One-Stop Shop (Guichet Unique). Pay the registration fees (approx 135,000 DJF total estimated).

steps.title: Publication
steps.description: Publish a notice of incorporation in the Official Journal or a legal announcements newspaper.

steps.title: Tax & Social Security Activation
steps.description: Obtain your NIF (Tax Activity Number) and Patent (Business License) from the Tax Directorate. Register with CNSS as an employer.

items.title: DIFTZ Free Zone
items.text: Companies in the Djibouti International Free Trade Zone (DIFTZ) enjoy 0% corporate tax, 0% VAT, and 0% customs duties, but can only trade internationally or with other Free Zone entities.

items.title: SARL vs SA
items.text: SARL (Limited Liability Company) is best for SMEs and subsidiaries. SA (Public Limited Company) is required for banking, insurance, and large public ventures, requiring a board of directors.

items.title: Local Address (Domiciliation)
items.text: A physical office presence (domiciliation) is strictly required for registration. P.O. boxes are not accepted as a registered address.

items.title: Manager Requirement
items.text: A SARL must have at least one manager (Gérant). The manager does not need to be a shareholder but must be a resident or hold a valid visa if foreign.

faqs.question: How long does the incorporation process take?
faqs.answer: The formal process via ODPIC takes about 3-7 days. However, bank account opening and finalizing tax registrations can add 2-3 weeks to the timeline.

faqs.question: Can foreigners own 100% of a company?
faqs.answer: Yes, Djibouti allows 100% foreign ownership in most sectors, provided the sector is not restricted (e.g., certain defense or mining activities).

faqs.question: What is the Patent tax?
faqs.answer: The 'Patente' is an annual business license tax divided into a fixed duty (based on activity type) and proportional duty (based on the rental value of business premises).

faqs.question: Do I need a local partner?
faqs.answer: Generally, no. A local partner is not mandatory for standard SARL registration unless specific sector regulations require it.

items.title: Chamber of Commerce
items.text: Registration with the Chambre de Commerce de Djibouti (CCD) is mandatory for importers and exporters.

items.title: Bank Account
items.text: Maintaining a local bank account is essential for tax payments and payroll. Top banks include BCIMR, EXIM Bank, and CAC Bank.

items.title: Official Stamp
items.text: Immediately after incorporation, commission your company stamp (Cachet). Nothing is official without it.

heroData.title: Staffing in Djibouti
heroData.subtitle: Recruit local and expat talent
heroData.description: Find skilled professionals in logistics, telecommunications, and finance in Djibouti's competitive talent market. Leverage local portals and agencies to build your team.

steps.title: Sourcing Strategy
steps.description: Advertise via ANEFIP (National Employment Agency), LinkedIn (growing usage), or local newspapers like 'La Nation'. Word of mouth is also powerful.

steps.title: Candidate Screening
steps.description: Conduct interviews. Bilingualism (French/English) is a premium skill in the logistics sector. Verify educational certificates.

steps.title: Contract Negotiation
steps.description: Agree on gross salary. Note that quoted salaries are often 'Net' in local custom, so clarify 'Gross' early.

steps.title: ANEFIP Declaration
steps.description: Mandatory declaration of the hiring to the National Agency for Employment, Training and Professional Integration (ANEFIP) to ensure local priority rules are met.

steps.title: Offer Letter
steps.description: Sign a formal offer letter detailing the terms, followed by the definitive employment contract.

items.title: Skills Availability
items.text: There is a high availability of logistics, port management, and administrative staff due to the Doraleh Port ecosystem. There is a shortage in advanced IT developers and specialized engineers.

items.title: Local Priority Laws
items.text: The law prioritizes Djiboutian nationals. You must effectively prove unavailability of local talent (ANEFIP certificate) before hiring an expatriate for a role.

items.title: University Partnerships
items.text: Partnerships with the University of Djibouti can be a good source for entry-level talent in business and engineering.

items.title: Formalities
items.text: Titles are important. Use 'Monsieur' or 'Madame' until invited to use first names. Handshakes are common but be mindful of cross-gender interactions in religious contexts.

items.title: Meetings
items.text: Initial meetings are often for relationship building. Do not rush to business immediately. Tea is often served and should be accepted.

items.title: Religious Observance
items.text: Avoid scheduling critical meetings on Fridays (Jummah) or during prayer times.

faqs.question: What is the standard probation period?
faqs.answer: Typically 15 days to 3 months depending on the role (worker vs executive), renewable once. It must be written in the contract.

faqs.question: Can I perform background checks?
faqs.answer: Yes, criminal records (Bulletin N°3 du Casier Judiciaire) are standard requests for positions of trust.

faqs.question: Are recruiting agencies regulated?
faqs.answer: Yes, agencies must be licensed. Using unlicensed brokers is risky.

items.title: Personal Connections
items.text: Djibouti is a relationship-based society. Referrals and 'wasta' (connections) often play a significant role in finding trustworthy staff.

items.title: Probationary Periods
items.text: Strict adherence to probationary limits (max 3 months for execs) is crucial; exceeding this automatically grants permanent status.

items.title: Notice Periods
items.text: Notice periods are lengthier than in many western jurisdictions, often reaching 3 months for senior management roles.

heroData.title: HRIS in Djibouti
heroData.subtitle: Digitize your HR Management
heroData.description: Adoption of HRIS systems is key for compliance with CNSS and new digital tax filing requirements. Modernize your workforce management.
heroData.bestFor: Medium to Large Enterprises with >20 employees

steps.title: Needs Assessment
steps.description: Ensure support for French language interface and DJF currency formatting.

steps.title: Vendor Selection
steps.description: Choose between global providers like Odoo (popular locally due to open source nature) or regional specialized software.

steps.title: Data Migration
steps.description: Migrate employee tax IDs (NIF), CNSS numbers, and accrued leave balances.

steps.title: Configuration
steps.description: Configure the specific Djibouti tax brackets and social security ceilings.

steps.title: Training
steps.description: Train HR staff on generating monthly reports for authorities.

items.title: Odoo ERP
items.text: Odoo is widely supported by local integrators in Djibouti for HR and Payroll modules and is cost-effective.

items.title: CNSS Integration
items.text: Look for systems that can export CNSS declaration files in the required format (or Excel compatible) to save manual entry time.

items.title: Data Hosting
items.text: Ensure your connectivity to the cloud host is reliable, as internet speeds can sometimes fluctuate, though fiber is generally good in the capital.

faqs.question: Is cloud HRIS secure?
faqs.answer: Yes, but ensure data residency compliance if dealing with sensitive government contracts.

faqs.question: Do I need biometrics?
faqs.answer: Biometric attendance is increasingly common in logistics and port operations.

faqs.question: Is training included?
faqs.answer: Most vendors charge separately for on-site training. Clarify this in your SLA.

items.title: Internet Infrastructure
items.text: Djibouti is a landing point for major subsea cables, meaning backbone connectivity is excellent, but local loop reliability varies.

items.title: Mobile First
items.text: Ensure your HRIS has a mobile-friendly interface; many employees will access self-service portals primarily via smartphones.

items.title: Language Localization
items.text: While French is official, an interface that supports intuitive icons or local languages (Somali/Afar) can boost adoption among blue-collar staff.

heroData.title: Accounting in Djibouti
heroData.subtitle: Maintain compliant books
heroData.description: Follow the Plan Comptable Général Djiboutien (PCGD) for all financial reporting. Ensure accuracy for tax audits.

steps.title: Bookkeeping
steps.description: Maintain daily records in French. Currency must be converted to accounting DJF using official daily rates.

steps.title: VAT Filing
steps.description: Monthly filing of VAT (10%) by the 20th of the following month.

steps.title: Interim Reviews
steps.description: Quarterly reviews are recommended to estimate provisional tax payments.

steps.title: Annual Closure
steps.description: Close books by Dec 31. Prepare Financial Statements (Bilan, Compte de Résultat).

steps.title: Audit & Submission
steps.description: Submit financials by March 31 (or April 30 in some cases) to the Tax Authority.

items.title: PCGD Standard
items.text: Djibouti uses its own General Chart of Accounts (PCGD - Plan Comptable Général Djiboutien), which is distinct from OHADA but shares some French accounting heritage.

items.title: Audit Requirement
items.text: SAs and SARLs above certain revenue thresholds must appoint a Statutory Auditor (Commissaire aux Comptes) to certify their accounts.

items.title: Software
items.text: Popular software includes Sage Saari and Odoo, configured for PCGD.

faqs.question: Can I keep books in English?
faqs.answer: For internal reporting yes, but official statutory accounts and ledgers demanded by tax authorities must be in French.

faqs.question: Are e-invoices mandatory?
faqs.answer: Djibouti is moving towards digitalization, but physical stamped invoices are still widely used and required for VAT reclamation.

faqs.question: What reporting currency is used?
faqs.answer: All statutory accounts must be maintained and reported in Djiboutian Francs (DJF).

items.title: Receipt Retention
items.text: Keep all original receipts. Scans are becoming more accepted but originals are preferred during physical audits.

items.title: Cash Economy
items.text: Petty cash usage is high. Implement strict controls and logbooks for all cash expenditures to ensure they are deductible.

items.title: Physical Stamps
items.text: The 'cachet' (company stamp) is essential. Almost every official accounting document requires a wet signature and stamp to be valid.

steps.title: UBO Declaration
steps.description: Identify and declare Ultimate Beneficial Owners to the registry.

steps.title: AML Policies
steps.description: Implement Anti-Money Laundering policies if in regulated sectors.

steps.title: Annual Filings
steps.description: Ensure annual legal secretariat filings (minutes of AGM) are deposited.

steps.title: License Renewals
steps.description: Track expiry of sector-specific licenses (e.g., transport, construction).

items.title: AML/CFT
items.text: Strict adherence to Central Bank of Djibouti AML guidelines is required for all financial transactions, given the regional context.

items.title: Corruption Index
items.text: While improved, navigating bureaucracy can present compliance risks. Maintain strict anti-bribery policies.

items.title: Sanctions Screening
items.text: Regularly screen local partners against international and regional sanctions lists, as the diverse port traffic increases exposure risk.

faqs.question: Is GDPR applicable?
faqs.answer: No, but Djibouti has its own emerging digital data laws (Loi sur la protection des données) that mirror some GDPR principles.

faqs.question: Can I operate without a license?
faqs.answer: No, operating without a 'Patente' or specific license can lead to immediate closure by authorities.

faqs.question: Are there sector-specific audits?
faqs.answer: Yes, sectors like banking, telecom, and logistics face more frequent compliance audits by their respective regulators.

items.title: Local Advisors
items.text: Having a local advisor who understands the unwritten rules of administration is often as important as knowing the written laws.

items.title: Bureaucratic Pace
items.text: Processes can be slow; build buffer time into all compliance timelines to account for administrative delays.

items.title: Ramadan Hours
items.text: Government offices have reduced hours during Ramadan, which significantly slows down processing times for licenses and permits.

steps.title: Registration
steps.description: Ensure NIF is active and tax center is assigned.

steps.title: Monthly Declarations
steps.description: Declare Payroll Tax and VAT by the 20th of each month.

steps.title: Minimum Tax Payment
steps.description: Pay the Minimum Lump Sum Tax (IMF) if applicable.

steps.title: Annual CIT Return
steps.description: File the Annual Corporate Income Tax return and pay balance by March 31.

items.title: Investment Code Incentives
items.text: The Investment Code offers tax holidays (5-7 years) for approved projects in strategic sectors like infrastructure, energy, and tourism.

items.title: Minimum Tax Rule
items.text: Even if loss-making, companies pay a minimum tax (Impôt Minimum Forfaitaire) of 1% of turnover, with a floor of 120,000 DJF.

items.title: Deductibility
items.text: Most business expenses are deductible, but strict limits apply to headquarters fees and certain provisions.

faqs.question: Is there a Double Tax Treaty?
faqs.answer: Djibouti has limited DTTs. Check with specific country agreements (e.g., France, Ethiopia) to avoid double taxation.

faqs.question: What is the VAT threshold?
faqs.answer: VAT registration is generally mandatory for annual turnover exceeding 20 Million DJF.

faqs.question: Are exports taxed?
faqs.answer: Exports are generally zero-rated for VAT.

items.title: Free Zone
items.text: Operating from the Free Zone is the most tax-efficient structure if your business model allows it (export-oriented).

items.title: Withholding Tax
items.text: Be aware of withholding tax on payments to foreign service providers (typically 10-25%), which applies if the provider is not a resident.

items.title: Tax Clearance
items.text: A Tax Clearance Certificate (Attestation de Situation Fiscale) is often required for bidding on public tenders or renewing licenses.

heroData.title: Legal & MSA in Djibouti
heroData.subtitle: Contractual frameworks
heroData.description: Master Service Agreements and local legal support. Secure your commercial relationships with robust contracts.

items.title: Civil Code
items.text: Contracts are governed by the Civil Code which is based on French civil law. Concepts like 'force majeure' are well recognized.

items.title: Dispute Resolution
items.text: Arbitration is increasingly popular (IGAD Business Forum or International Arbitration centers) due to potential delays in local commercial courts.

items.title: Notarization
items.text: Certain contracts (real estate/commercial leases) require notarization to be enforceable.

steps.title: Scope Definition
steps.description: Clearly define deliverables and acceptance criteria.

steps.title: Governing Law
steps.description: Ideally choose Djibouti law for local assets, or a neutral venue (Paris/London arbitration) for international dealings.

steps.title: Language Clause
steps.description: Specify the prevailing language in case of dispute (usually French).

steps.title: Execution
steps.description: Signatures should be witnessed. For high value, register the contract.

faqs.question: Can I use English law?
faqs.answer: You can, but enforcement in local Djiboutian courts may be complex and require translation and validation.

faqs.question: Are digital signatures valid?
faqs.answer: Validity is improving with new electronic transaction laws, but wet ink is still safest for major contracts.

faqs.question: Can I terminate early?
faqs.answer: Yes, but French civil law protects against 'abusive termination'. Ensure your cause is well-documented.

items.title: Law Firms
items.text: Several international law firms have associations or presences in Djibouti due to the port and military bases.

items.title: Stamp Duty
items.text: Contracts often attract registration fees and stamp duties (Droits d'Enregistrement) to be admissible in local court.

items.title: Termination Clauses
items.text: Be explicit about termination conditions. French civil law protects parties from 'abusive termination', so cause must be clearly documented.

heroData.title: Software in Djibouti
heroData.subtitle: Tech landscape
heroData.description: IT services and internet infrastructure providers. Sourcing technology for your local operations.

items.title: Subsea Cables
items.text: Djibouti is a major landing station for 8+ submarine cables, offering some of the best connectivity backbones in Africa, though last-mile can be pricey.

items.title: Monopoly
items.text: Djibouti Telecom is the state-owned monopoly provider. Service options are limited compared to competitive markets.

items.title: 5G Rollout
items.text: 5G trials have begun in Djibouti City (2025), targeting logistics and port zones first.

items.title: Last Mile Cost
items.text: While the backbone is strong, last-mile fiber connectivity can still be relatively pricey for businesses compared to global standards.

steps.title: Identify Vendor
steps.description: Local integrators exist for Cisco/Microsoft.

steps.title: Licensing
steps.description: Ensure software licenses are valid for the Africa region to avoid activation issues.

steps.title: Installation
steps.description: Coordinate with local IT support for physical installation if hardware is involved.

steps.title: Import Duties
steps.description: Check if hardware import duties apply (typically high unless in Free Zone).

steps.title: Installation
steps.description: Arrange for local installation support.

faqs.question: Is 5G available?
faqs.answer: Djibouti Telecom has started rolling out 4G+/5G trials.

faqs.question: Are there local data centers?
faqs.answer: Yes, the Djibouti Data Center (DDC) is a Tier 3 certified facility serving the region.

faqs.question: Can I import hardware?
faqs.answer: Yes, but customs duties are high (approx 33% cumulative) unless you have an exoneration.

items.title: Regional Hub
items.text: Djibouti aims to be the 'Singapore of Africa' for digital connectivity due to its cable landings.

items.title: Power Stability
items.text: While improving, power fluctuations can occur. UPS and stabilizers are recommended for server rooms.

items.title: Local Talent
items.text: There is a growing pool of young IT professionals, but senior specialized expertise may need to be expatriated.

heroData.title: Marketing in Djibouti
heroData.subtitle: Localize your brand
heroData.description: Reach audiences via Radio, TV (RTD), and Digital channels. Adapt your message to the cultural nuances of Djibouti.

items.title: Social Media
items.text: Facebook is the dominant platform. WhatsApp marketing is highly effective.

items.title: Television
items.text: RTD (Radiodiffusion Télévision de Djibouti) is the sole national broadcaster, offering channels in French, Arabic, Somali, and Afar.

items.title: Billboards
items.text: Outdoor advertising is very popular in Djibouti City, especially along the Venice Road and Port areas.

items.title: Traditional Media
items.text: Radio (RTD) remains very popular for reaching mass audiences outside the capital.

steps.title: Localization
steps.description: Translate assets to French and Somali/Afar for broader reach.

steps.title: Approvals
steps.description: Ensure content complies with moral and religious standards.

steps.title: Media Buying
steps.description: Book slots directly with RTD or via local agencies for TV/Radio.

steps.title: Channel Selection
steps.description: Choose between digital (younger demographic) and radio/billboard (general public).

steps.title: Compliance
steps.description: Ensure ads comply with cultural sensitivities.

faqs.question: Are there local influencers?
faqs.answer: Yes, micro-influencers on TikTok/Instagram are growing.

faqs.question: Is print media effective?
faqs.answer: La Nation is the main government newspaper and is effective for official announcements and B2B.

faqs.question: Are there content restrictions?
faqs.answer: Yes, alcohol and gambling advertising is restricted or banned due to Islamic norms.

items.title: Cultural Sensitivity
items.text: Visuals should be modest and respectful of Islamic traditions. Avoid imagery that could be considered offensive.

items.title: Language Mix
items.text: Campaigns are often trilingual: French for business/formal, Somali/Afar for mass market appeal.

items.title: Word of Mouth
items.text: Djibouti is a small community. Reputation spreads fast, making customer service a key marketing channel.
